narrative:
The model predicted a 62.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this decision, ranked by importance. Your undergraduate GPA was the strongest influence. At 3.40 it sits above the 3.23 average of accepted students, yet the model still saw it as increasing your risk of failure. This suggests the system weighs even solid grades less favorably when other academic signals are mixed.

Your performance in the third year of law school came next. Placing in the 9th decile is excellent—well above the 5.79 average among accepted students—and this record pushed the prediction toward passing. However, its favorable effect was not large enough to overcome the other signals.

Family income ranked third. Being from an upper-middle income background, which is the most common bracket among accepted students (45%), still nudged the outcome slightly toward failure in the model’s logic.

Taken together, these pieces led the system to conclude you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam. To improve your chances on a future application, focus on strengthening every academic signal you can control—especially consistent high performance across all years of law school and targeted bar-prep work that demonstrates first-time passage potential. Reapply once you have clearer evidence of bar exam readiness. (248 words)
